sections.relationship: Students mix up turns and flips because the whole shape changes position. Following one distinctive cell (and which way the shape bends from it) separates turns from flips.
sections.author_note: Students mix up turns and flips because the whole shape changes position. Following one distinctive cell (and which way the shape bends from it) separates turns from flips.

lesson.title: Follow one marked corner
text: Pick one distinctive cell of the shape, for example the end of its longest arm, and note which way the shape bends from there (clockwise or counterclockwise).
A turn moves that cell around but keeps the bending direction the same.
A flip reverses the bending direction. If the direction is reversed, the figure is a mirror image and no turn can produce it (unless the shape is symmetric).
For a quarter-turn clockwise, the top of the shape goes to the right side; for a half-turn, the top goes to the bottom and left goes to right.

example.title: Worked example (a different shape)
prompt: An L made of 3 cells going down and 1 cell to the right at the bottom. Where does the single cell go after a half-turn?
steps: After a half-turn, the bottom goes to the top and the right goes to the left.
So the single cell ends up at the TOP, on the LEFT: the shape looks like a "7" made of cells.
Bending direction: going down the long arm, the foot turns left (counterclockwise) in the original and still turns the same way after the half-turn, so it is a turn, not a flip.
